opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the answer has shifted quite a bit as the models have changed.

In the earlier generation of systems, where you had a separate text encoder feeding a diffusion model, prompt rewriting was almost a necessity. Users would type something short like "a cat on a skateboard," and the model had been trained on these long, dense, descriptive captions. So there was a distribution mismatch. A rewriter, usually a language model, would expand that into the kind of detailed caption the image model actually expected, and quality went up a lot. It was basically a bridge between how people talk and how the model was trained.

When you move to a more integrated model, where the same system that understands language is also producing the image, a lot of that bridging happens inside the model. It already has the world knowledge and the reasoning to infer what you probably meant. So the explicit rewrite step becomes less about fixing a mismatch and more of a design choice.

I'd frame it as a trade-off between helpfulness and control. Rewriting can fill in sensible details like lighting, composition and style, and for casual users that's usually great. But it also adds the system's own assumptions. If you're a power user who wrote a very precise prompt, you don't want something quietly changing it. And on things like diversity or style defaults, the rewriter is where many of those decisions get made, sometimes in ways people find surprising.

So my view is that in an integrated model the "rewriting" is better thought of as the model reasoning about intent before it generates, kind of like thinking before answering. Ideally that's adaptive: elaborate when the request is underspecified, stay faithful when it's specific. Being somewhat transparent about it helps too, so people can see how their request was interpreted and push back. Conversation makes that much easier, because you can just say "no, not like that" and iterate, instead of trying to get everything into one perfect prompt.

r001.rationale: The response describes a language-model rewriter expanding short prompts to match the captions expected by an earlier image model. It does not say the rewriter conveys the language model’s world knowledge to a text-only image model.

r002.rationale: It says that with an integrated model, much of the bridging happens inside the model, so the explicit rewrite step is less necessary.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually a question I get a lot, and I think the answer has shifted pretty dramatically in the last couple of years. If you go back to the earlier text-to-image systems, prompt rewriting was almost a crutch. You had a diffusion model with a relatively weak text encoder, something like CLIP, and it just didn't understand language very well. So you'd put a language model in front of it that would take "a cat on a skateboard" and expand it into this long, florid paragraph with lighting descriptions and camera lenses and all of that, because the image model responded better to that kind of dense description. The rewriter was essentially translating from how people talk into the dialect the image model happened to speak.

With an integrated model, where the language understanding and the image generation are part of the same system, that motivation mostly goes away. The model already understands what you mean. It can handle long instructions, it can handle short ones, it can do multi-turn editing where you say "okay, now make the cat orange" and it knows what "the cat" refers to. So the question becomes: is there still a role for rewriting, or is it just baggage?

And my view is that there's still a role, but it's a different one. It's less about translation and more about intent. When someone types a short prompt, there's a lot that's unspecified. What aspect ratio, what style, what's in the background, is this photorealistic or illustrated. A good system has to fill in those gaps somehow, and you can either do that implicitly, where the model's priors just decide, or you can do it explicitly, where there's a step that reasons about what the user probably wants. The explicit version has some real advantages. It's inspectable, you can show the user what the system thought they meant, and you can steer it. If you're building a product and you know your users mostly want a certain look, you can bake that in without retraining the generator.

The thing I'd caution against is rewriting that fights the user. There's a failure mode where someone writes a very precise prompt, they know exactly what they want, and the rewriter "helpfully" adds a bunch of stuff that changes the result. That's really frustrating. So the way I think about it now is that rewriting should be adaptive. If the prompt is sparse, do more. If the prompt is detailed, do very little, maybe just fix obvious ambiguities. And ideally the model itself learns that behavior, so it's not a separate bolt-on component at all, it's just part of how the model interprets instructions.

The other place it still matters is safety and policy, honestly. Having a step that reasons about the request before pixels get generated is useful, and that's separate from image quality. But I'd keep those concerns distinct, because conflating "rewrite for quality" and "rewrite for policy" tends to make both worse.

r001.rationale: The response describes rewriting as translating prompts for older image models with weak text encoders. It does not say the purpose is to convey a language model’s world knowledge to an image model that accepts only text.

r002.rationale: The response says that with an integrated model, the motivation for rewriting “mostly goes away,” clearly stating that integration reduces the need for it.

astra-6.text:
I think of prompt rewriting as a way to bridge what a person asks for and what the image generator needs to produce a useful result. People often express an intent without specifying every visual detail, so some interpretation is necessary. The challenge is deciding which details help express that intent and which ones change it.

With an integrated model, that interpretation can happen in the context of the conversation. If we've been discussing a particular style or composition, the model can carry that into the image request without making you repeat everything. An explicit prompt rewrite is one way to do that, but it isn't necessarily a separate step you need to expose to the user.

The important thing is preserving control. If you're very specific, the model should respect that specificity. If your request is open-ended, it has more room to make creative choices. A more elaborate prompt isn't automatically a better prompt; what matters is whether the resulting image reflects what you meant.

r001.rationale: The response describes interpreting a person’s intent for the image generator, but does not say prompt rewriting conveys a language model’s world knowledge to a text-only image model.

r002.rationale: It says an integrated model can carry conversational context into an image request without requiring the user to repeat it, and that an explicit rewrite need not be a separate step.

sol-6.1.text:
I think prompt rewriting is really an interface between what the user says and what the image generation model needs. A user might give you a very short request, but there’s often intent in the surrounding conversation that should inform the image. With an integrated model, you have the opportunity to use that context directly, rather than treating every image request as an isolated prompt.

The tricky part is deciding how much to elaborate. You want to fill in details that make the image useful, but you don’t want to override the user’s intent. If they specify a particular composition or style, those constraints need to survive. So I’d think of rewriting less as making the prompt longer and more as translating the user’s intent faithfully into something the image generator can act on. Ideally, the user doesn’t have to think about that translation at all.

r001.rationale: The response describes translating user intent and conversational context into a prompt, but does not say rewriting conveys the language model’s world knowledge to a text-only image model.

r002.rationale: It says an integrated model can use context directly, but does not state that integration reduces the need for prompt rewriting.
